## Research area: Bridging Informal and Formal Mathematical Reasoning — Autoformalization and Proof Verification

    "title": "Olympiad-Level Formal Mathematical Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning",
    "venue": "Nature 2025",
    "problem_identification": "The authors identified a fundamental tension: LLMs doing math in natural language can hallucinate plausible but incorrect reasoning steps, while formal theorem provers guarantee correctness but are starved for training data (~300k human-written tactic pairs in all of Mathlib). Prior work either scaled informal reasoning (risking correctness) or stayed small-scale in formal settings (limiting capability). The key gap was: no one had figured out how to generate enough formal training signal to make RL work at the scale needed for olympiad-level problems. They found this gap by recognizing that formal verification provides a perfect, non-gameable reward signal — analogous to the win/lose outcome in Go — but the 'game board' (formal math) lacked the self-play data generation loop that made AlphaZero work.",
    "key_insight": "Two interlocked insights made this work: (1) Formal verification is the mathematical equivalent of a game engine — it provides a binary, incorruptible reward signal that enables AlphaZero-style RL without any human proof supervision, and (2) the training data bottleneck can be shattered by autoformalization at scale — using Gemini to translate 1M informal math problems into ~80M formal Lean statements, creating an unprecedented self-generating curriculum. The combination transforms theorem proving from a data-scarce supervised learning problem into a data-rich RL problem.",
    "innovation_type": "combination",
    "method_summary": "AlphaProof is a 3B-parameter encoder-decoder transformer with dual policy (tactic generation) and value (proof difficulty estimation) heads, trained in four stages: (1) pretraining on 300B tokens of code/math, (2) supervised fine-tuning on 300k Mathlib state-tactic pairs, (3) autoformalization via fine-tuned Gemini 1.5 Pro to generate ~80M formal Lean problems from 1M informal statements, and (4) large-scale RL (~80,000 TPU-days) using AlphaZero-style tree search with PUCT selection, AND-node decomposition for multi-goal states, and a matchmaker curriculum system that routes problems based on 'interestingness.' The critical innovation is Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL): at inference, the system generates diverse formal variants (simplifications, generalizations) of the target problem and runs focused RL training on this synthetic curriculum, adding ~15 percentage points over tree search alone at the cost of 2-3 TPU-days per problem. Every candidate proof is verified by Lean's type checker, ensuring only correct proofs are accepted.",
    "what_makes_it_good": "This paper earns Nature by combining an extraordinary empirical result (solving 4/6 IMO 2024 problems including P6, which only 5 humans solved) with a guarantee no prior AI math system could offer: formal correctness. The result is instantly legible to non-experts ('AI wins silver medal at Math Olympiad') while being technically rigorous — every proof is machine-verified against only three accepted axioms. The TTRL paradigm is a genuinely novel contribution to the field, showing that RL can be productively applied not just during training but as an inference-time strategy, and the 80M-problem autoformalization pipeline establishes a new scale for formal mathematics datasets. The paper also demonstrates remarkable intellectual honesty about compute costs and limitations, which strengthens rather than weakens the contribution.",
    "limitations_acknowledged": "The authors explicitly flag five limitations: (1) massive computational cost (280,000+ TPU-days total, multi-day inference per hard problem), raising 'important questions about accessibility and the future of an open research ecosystem'; (2) the system operates within competition mathematics, not research-frontier problems or 'theory building'; (3) combinatorics remains a weak domain (20.3% vs 72.6% algebra on formal-imo); (4) the IMO evaluation used extended time far beyond the human 4.5-hour limit; and (5) mathematical 'taste, interestingness, or beauty' remain beyond the system's grasp.",
    "open_questions": [
      "Can TTRL-style test-time adaptation be made efficient enough to be practical without multi-day TPU budgets? The logarithmic scaling of tree search suggests diminishing returns — is there a way to get superlinear scaling, perhaps through better curriculum generation or meta-learning?",

Is this a fundamental limitation of the Lean formalization ecosystem (fewer combinatorial lemmas in Mathlib), a property of the RL training distribution, or evidence that combinatorial reasoning requires qualitatively different search strategies?",
      "Can autoformalization quality be improved beyond 60% success on IMO problems? The current pipeline loses ~40% of problems in translation — closing this gap could unlock substantial capability gains without any changes to the RL system itself. More broadly, can we build bidirectional autoformalization that also translates formal proofs back into human-readable insights?"

For our research area, the key lessons are: (1) autoformalization is the critical bottleneck — at 60% success rate, improving it is arguably higher-leverage than improving the prover; (2) formal verification transforms the learning problem from 'judge quality of reasoning' to 'binary correct/incorrect,' which is a profound simplification for RL; and (3) TTRL shows that the boundary between training and inference is dissolving — systems can learn specifically for the problem at hand, redefining what 'generalization' means in formal reasoning."

    "title": "Lean-STaR: Learning to Interleave Thinking and Proving",
    "venue": "ICLR 2025 (Spotlight)",
    "problem_identification": "The authors identified that formal theorem proving datasets (e.g., Mathlib for Lean) contain only tactic sequences with no informal reasoning traces, yet human mathematicians rely heavily on informal intuition before writing formal steps. The gap is structural: interactive theorem provers produce (state, tactic) pairs, but the 'why' behind each tactic is never recorded. They found this gap by observing that chain-of-thought reasoning dramatically helps in mathematical word problems but had never been applied at the per-step level in formal theorem proving — the informal-formal bridge was missing precisely where it would be most useful.",
    "key_insight": "You don't need naturally-occurring thought-tactic pairs to train a 'thinking prover' — you can synthesize them retrospectively by asking an oracle LLM (GPT-4) to rationalize ground-truth tactics after the fact, then use the formal verifier's binary correctness signal (proof compiles or doesn't) to filter and bootstrap the quality of these synthetic thoughts via expert iteration. The formal system itself becomes the quality assurance mechanism for informal reasoning.",
    "innovation_type": "combination",
    "method_summary": "Lean-STaR operates in three phases. Phase 1 (SFT): fine-tune a base LLM on standard (proof-state, tactic) pairs from Mathlib to get a competent tactic predictor. Phase 2 (Thought Augmentation): for each (state, ground-truth tactic) pair, use GPT-4 to retrospectively generate a plausible natural-language rationale that would precede that tactic, creating ~52K (state, thought, tactic) triples; then fine-tune the model to generate thought→tactic sequences, factoring the generation as π(thought|state) × π(tactic|thought, state). Phase 3 (Expert Iteration): sample K proof trajectories per theorem using the thought-augmented model, retain only those that Lean verifies as correct, and fine-tune on the union of original and successful new data; repeat for multiple rounds. Critically, at inference time they abandon best-first search in favor of parallel sampling, because log-probability scoring breaks down when variable-length natural language thoughts inflate the sequence — this sampling-based evaluation was itself a methodological contribution.",

Third, the paper contributes a reusable artifact (the first thought-augmented theorem proving dataset at scale) and demonstrates that the approach composes with stronger base models, suggesting generality rather than overfitting to one configuration.",

They also note dependence on GPT-4 for initial thought synthesis, which introduces cost and potential bias. The improvement margin (43.4%→46.3%) is meaningful but modest, and the approach has not yet been tested on benchmarks beyond miniF2F.",

Is this because per-step formal proving is already inherently sequential, or because the synthetic thoughts are lower quality than human-written rationales? Understanding this gap could unlock much larger improvements.",

The area chair noted all major concerns were adequately addressed in rebuttals and recommended spotlight acceptance.",
    "relevance_to_seed": "This paper is directly at the core of bridging informal and formal reasoning — it literally operationalizes the bridge by interleaving natural language thoughts with formal tactics at each proof step. For our research area, the key transferable lessons are: (1) retrospective synthesis is a powerful technique for creating training data that bridges modalities (informal↔formal) when naturally paired data doesn't exist; (2) formal verification provides a free, high-quality reward signal that can bootstrap the quality of informal reasoning — this insight generalizes well beyond theorem proving to any autoformalization task where one side has a verifier."

    "title": "Rethinking and Improving Autoformalization: Towards a Faithful Metric and a Dependency Retrieval-based Approach",
    "venue": "ICLR 2025 (Spotlight)",
    "problem_identification": "The authors identified two fundamental gaps by critically re-examining the entire autoformalization pipeline rather than just trying to improve translation accuracy. First, they observed that ALL existing automated evaluation metrics are unfaithful proxies: BLEU is fragile to semantics-preserving transformations (e.g., β-reduction), type-checking is necessary but not sufficient, and LLM graders are non-deterministic and prompt-dependent. Second, they diagnosed that the dominant failure mode — hallucinated formal identifiers and definitions — stems from models being context-blind to what already exists in formal libraries. The key methodological move was stepping back to ask 'are we even measuring the right thing?' before trying to optimize performance.",
    "key_insight": "Definitional equality in dependent type theory (Lean 4) already provides a principled, formally-grounded equivalence relation that is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and partially aligned with human intuition — but it is too strict. The 'aha' was recognizing you can extend it into a practical evaluation metric by (1) adding a restricted set of tactic-based transformation primitives and (2) using an LLM to search for transformation proofs, then verifying them symbolically. This creates a neuro-symbolic hybrid where the neural component handles search flexibility while the symbolic component guarantees formal soundness. You don't invent equivalence from scratch — you loosen an existing formal concept just enough.",
    "innovation_type": "combination",
    "method_summary": "BEq (Bidirectional Extended Definitional Equivalence) checks whether two formal statements are equivalent by testing both directions: can s_P be transformed to be definitionally equal to s_Q, and vice versa? The transformation function T uses an LLM (InternLM-Math-Plus-20B, 5-shot prompted) to generate tactic sequences from a restricted set R = {apply, cases', constructor, exact, exact?, ext, have, intro, intros, rw, use}, which are then symbolically verified in the Lean 4 kernel. For autoformalization itself, RAutoformalizer parses dependency graphs across all 243,797 formal objects in Mathlib 4, topologically informalizes them (bottom-up through 24 generations using LLM informalization), trains a dense retriever (fine-tuned BGE-M3 with hard negatives) to retrieve relevant dependencies given an informal statement, and conditions a fine-tuned autoformalizer (InternLM2-Math-Base-7B) on both the informal statement and top-5 retrieved dependencies. A novel OOD benchmark, Con-NF (961 pairs from a New Foundations consistency proof library), tests generalization beyond Mathlib 4.",
    "what_makes_it_good": "This paper succeeds because it attacks the evaluation problem and the generation problem simultaneously with a unified philosophy: formal methods should ground both measurement and generation. BEq is not just a metric — it's a formally provable equivalence relation (the authors prove reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity) validated against expert human judgments (90.50% accuracy, 100% precision on 200 expert-labeled pairs). The paper's scope is unusually comprehensive for a single submission: a new metric with formal guarantees, a new retrieval paradigm with a novel training data synthesis pipeline (topological informalization), AND a new OOD benchmark — each alone could be a contribution, but together they tell a coherent story about rethinking the entire autoformalization workflow.",
    "limitations_acknowledged": "BEq depends on the quality of ground-truth formal statements and cannot be applied to benchmarks lacking formal ground-truths. Its recall is limited by the rigor of formal verification systems and the approximated transformation function (the LLM). For RAutoformalizer, high-ranking retrievals are the main bottleneck; the oracle retrieval experiment (RA +R) shows massive headroom (e.g., 31.28% vs 16.86% BEq@8 on Con-NF), and sophisticated retrieval upgrades like multi-vector embeddings, re-ranking, and query augmentation are left as future work.",

    "reviewer_feedback_summary": "Reviewers praised BEq's originality and formal grounding ('grounded in human intuitions about equivalence'), the topological informalization pipeline's cleverness, and the new OOD benchmark's rigor. After rebuttals, all reviewers moved to accept, with one noting 'revisions have strengthened the paper's clarity.' The Area Chair concluded: 'This paper makes significant contribution to autoformalization and formal mathematics, introducing a reliable evaluation metric, innovative technique, and benchmark for OOD generalization.'",
    "relevance_to_seed": "This paper is directly central to our research area — it provides both the evaluation infrastructure (BEq) and generation methodology (retrieval-augmented autoformalization) needed to bridge informal and formal mathematical reasoning. The key transferable lessons are: (1) before improving a system, first fix how you measure it (BEq exposed that prior metrics were deeply unfaithful), (2) grounding neural methods in formal verification primitives creates hybrid systems that are both flexible and sound, and (3) treating autoformalization as a retrieval-augmented problem that respects the dependency structure of formal libraries is a paradigm shift from treating it as pure sequence-to-sequence translation."

  {
    "title": "MUSTARD: Mastering Uniform Synthesis of Theorem and Proof Data",
    "venue": "ICLR 2024 (Spotlight)",
    "problem_identification": "The authors identified a three-way tension in mathematical reasoning data: manual annotation (miniF2F) is correct but tiny, rule-based synthesis (INT) is validated but semantically meaningless, and LLM-generated data (ROSCOE-style) is meaningful but unverified. No existing pipeline could produce data that was simultaneously large-scale, semantically meaningful, AND formally verified. They found this gap by systematically categorizing prior data sources along three axes—scale, correctness, and meaningfulness—and noticing no method covered all three.",
    "key_insight": "Use the LLM as a creative generator of mathematically meaningful problems (leveraging its broad knowledge) but use a formal proof assistant (Lean) as an incorruptible filter—then feed Lean's error messages back to the LLM for iterative self-correction. The insight is that you don't need the LLM to be correct; you need a verification oracle that rejects bad outputs and an error-feedback loop that recovers salvageable ones. This turns the LLM's unreliability from a bug into a feature: failed-then-corrected proofs naturally produce harder, more interesting examples.",
    "innovation_type": "combination",
    "method_summary": "MUSTARD operates in three stages. (1) Concept Seeding: uniformly sample 1–2 mathematical concepts from a Khan Academy-derived pool of 274 concepts spanning four difficulty levels (elementary through higher education) across algebra, geometry, calculus, and statistics. (2) LLM Generation: prompt GPT-4 with the sampled concepts to generate a triple—informal problem statement (T1), natural language proof (T2), and Lean 3 formal proof (T3)—deliberately without few-shot exemplars to maximize diversity. Generation uses role-separated prompting: a 'math expert' persona for T1/T2 and a 'Lean master' persona for T3. (3) Iterative Validation: compile the Lean proof; if it fails, feed the error messages with line numbers back to GPT-4 for targeted correction over multiple rounds. Only proofs passing Lean validation enter the final dataset. This produces MUSTARDSAUCE: 5,866 verified triples of informal-statement/informal-proof/formal-proof.",

Second, the human evaluation was unusually rigorous for a dataset paper—200 samples evaluated across six dimensions with statistical significance tests (p<0.005), directly demonstrating that formal-prover filtering causally improves informal proof quality. Third, the downstream utility was demonstrated comprehensively: fine-tuning Llama 2-7B yielded +15.4% on automated theorem proving and +8.2% on math word problems, with scalability ablations showing no saturation—the data keeps helping as you add more.",

    "title": "Autoformalize Mathematical Statements by Symbolic Equivalence and Semantic Consistency",
    "venue": "NeurIPS 2024",
    "problem_identification": "The authors identified a striking but under-exploited gap between pass@1 and pass@k accuracy in LLM-generated formalizations (19.5–26.5% on MATH and miniF2F). They found this gap through straightforward empirical measurement—plotting pass@k curves and observing that even GPT-4 jumps from ~37.5% pass@1 to ~53.5% pass@10 on MATH. The key realization was that the bottleneck isn't generation quality but rather verification and ranking of candidates.",
    "key_insight": "Self-consistency voting, proven effective in chain-of-thought reasoning, cannot be naïvely applied to formal math statements because variable declarations are inconsistent across generations and no test cases exist for execution-based checking. The core insight is to decompose consistency checking into two complementary, independently computable signals—symbolic equivalence (logical structure via ATPs) and semantic consistency (meaning preservation via back-translation embeddings)—that cover each other's blind spots across different mathematical domains.",
    "innovation_type": "combination",
    "method_summary": "Given k autoformalization candidates from an LLM, the framework scores each candidate along two axes. (2) Semantic Consistency: each candidate is back-translated (informalized) to natural language, and cosine similarity between BERT embeddings of the back-translation and the original statement measures meaning preservation. The two scores are normalized via softmax and combined using a log-linear combination with a balancing hyperparameter α (sweet spot: 0.32–0.6). The highest-scoring candidate is selected as the final formalization.",
